CD Projekt Red has announced that just today, November 24, the Polish studio signed newly introduced deals with Sony Interactive Entertainment for The Witcher 4's upcoming marketing campaign, among other efforts.

CFO Piotr Nielubowicz told investors that the deals cover CD Projekt Red's games on PlayStation and in the PlayStation Plus catalog, as well as "our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign.".

“This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years," he said, according to VGC.

No specifics were made available, but the partnership for The Witcher 4's marketing campaign has people theorizing that it could be similar to Rockstar's co-marketing deal with Sony for GTA 6.

Under that agreement, GTA 6 was marketed as a game that "plays best on PS5," even if the jury is out on that being true. Sony also created special GTA 6 DualSense controllers and even custom consoles for NBA players. The PlayStation branding was prioritized over Xbox to give people the impression that they should get it on PlayStation.

The Witcher 4 is in the works now and is expected to launch in 2028 for console and PC. The game kicks off a new trilogy of The Witcher games, which will also include The Witcher 5 and The Witcher 6. These will all be released within a six-year window, so the whole new trilogy could be out by 2034.

The studio is “targeting” a 2028 release for The Witcher 4, so it could be delayed like The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 were before it.

The Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

Image credit: NASA/Luke Delaney.

Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (TechCrunch)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
  • The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
  • Sources indicate that song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous tech giant to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.

The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.

Sources indicate that song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous tech giant to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.

Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.

The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big Tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.

“We take care of everything,” Han remarked. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”.

According to recent reports, everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.

Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.

Sources indicate that because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, major League Baseball sued its players’ association in federal court on Wednesday, asking that its contemplated lockout next week be declared legal and trying to head off any attempt by the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case. In a 38-page complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, MLB and the corporate entities owning its 30 teams sued the Major League Baseball Players Association and the eight players on the union’s executive subcommittee, including record-setting pitcher Tarik Skubal. “MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement (‘CBA’) at the bargaining table, where federal law claims it belongs,” the lawsuit says. “MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the Union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation.” Baseball’s five-year labor contract expires at 11:59 p.m. Dec. 1 and owners are expected to immediately impose a lockout, which would be the sport’s 10th work stoppage since 1972. Owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years. Owners asked for a declaratory judgment determining a lockout doesn’t violate antitrust laws and doesn’t amount to an unreasonable restraint of trade. They asked for a ruling that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin a lockout and for an order that the players be defined as a legal class, which if granted could block individual lawsuits. “The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous,” the union said in a statement. “We will respond appropriately, but MLB’s decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.” Among the lawyers representing MLB are former Solicitor General Paul D. Clement and Keker, Van Nest & Peters, which worked on behalf of the union in litigation against government seizure of drug tests. “Today’s filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season,” MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. “We believe the union is preparing to follow the playbook its new leadership has used against other major professional sports leagues by pretending to ‘disclaim’ its status as the players’ bargaining process.” Caplin referred decertification as a “nuclear option,” mirroring union head Bruce Meyer’s description of the salary cap proposal as a “nuclear bomb.” —Ronald Blum, AP baseball writer.

“MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement (‘CBA’) at the bargaining table, where federal law says it belongs,” the lawsuit says. “MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the Union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up. It doesn’t matter who you planned to vote for, the video struck an emotional—and negative—response. The clip was not AI-generated; the candidate really uttered the words you found upsetting. But the story the video told was fundamentally false. That was the 2026 midterms. Candidates and their supporters spent a whopping $80 million to make AI-generated ads, as part of what AdImpact projected will be the most expensive election cycle on record. This is one attempt to capture eyeballs and sway voters. Another is through foreign interference. In just one example, researchers tracking a Russian influence operation recently found a fake video masquerading as a Mother Jones report that captured over 11 million views. But disinformation is not stopping at deepfakes. Authentic videos that are repurposed and stripped of context represent a new frontier. I am not talking about a mere twisting of words. What we’re seeing is next level. THE NEW LOOK OF DISINFORMATION Think about the recent catastrophic flooding in Nepal and India. Some footage released within hours of the floods, intended to showcase the magnitude of the disaster, turned out to be from entirely different events. The footage was authentic. It just happened to be from a glacial flood in Alaska, a landslide in Japan, or a flood that occurred years before. These videos racked up millions of views. They also caused panic among friends and relatives trying to find information about their missing loved ones, and they potentially hindered rescue efforts by confusing the locations where help was needed. Now, consider the same tactic applied in the political sphere—real speeches and words taken drastically out of context, coming from events that could have happened years earlier. One of the most notable examples involved Michigan’s recently elected Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed. In August, he was eviscerated by Republicans for apparently calling for Sharia law to take over in America. Social media went crazy. Was the clip real? Yes, it was from a speech he gave in 2022. But the meaning was quite different when you look at its entirety in context. So different that Politifact gave it a “pants on fire” rating for its meaning being distorted. In Georgia’s hotly contested Senate race, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff ran an ad of Republican Mike Collins urging Americans to get off Social Security and return to work. But that’s not exactly how it went down. The audio came from a broader conversation about tax policy, government revenue, and workforce participation. Collins was not saying retirees should get back into the workforce and lose their benefits (Politifact rated this one as “mostly false”). In both cases, the recordings were authentic. The misleading impressions came from stripping away the information necessary to understand what was being noted, not from manipulating the original material. You may believe that this is just par for the course in a political campaign, but just because something is common does not make it safe, normal, or acceptable. THE IMPORTANCE OF CONTEXTUAL UNDERSTANDING This tactic is becoming effective for two main reasons. Video is now our most prominent data source. Everything is recorded, so if someone is looking for a soundbite to make someone look bad, there is plenty of material available, if they’re willing to dig for it. The second concern is more technical. Deepfake detectors look for signs of manipulation. Authentic videos pass that test. Determining whether a clip is deliberately misleading requires a new set of inquiries, identifying when and where the video took place, what was happening around it, and what the broader context revealed. Making such determinations traditionally has taken a lot of people a lot of time to dig through archives. Even with the deep war chests candidates possess, they’re not going to devote the human resources needed to debunk every false video, at least not in time for that work to make a dent in the video’s impact. So, campaigns take hits, and candidates can spend considerable time and energy trying to explain past comments and rebuild trust. WHAT’S THE FIX? In 2026, voters and media companies are learning that two things can simultaneously be true: A clip can be legitimate while what it depicts is inaccurate. Voters are overwhelmed with election messages. Expecting them to research every clip they see is highly unlikely. Candidates and their backers count on this. Media companies and social platforms bear a greater responsibility, however. Fact-checking and moderation capabilities are essential to reduce the rapid spread of disinformation. Interestingly, while generative AI can be used to create convincing fakes, a different application of AI can be a powerful tool for identifying misleading content and stopping its spread. As good as AI is getting at generating realistic videos, it’s also getting good at understanding them. Solutions that can read a video and its contextual clues can be indispensable in determining whether an authentic video is being misrepresented online. Imagine an instant army of agent fact-checkers. When AI understands video the way a human does, it recognizes not only what is said and who’s speaking, but what else is on the screen and what the setting looks like. It can also search massive archives to see if that moment has appeared anywhere else. And, at the agent layer, tech can flag suspicious content, assembling supporting evidence and escalating cases to human reviewers in minutes. The technology that helps media companies and platforms find original footage, restore full context, and flag misleading claims will enable a faster response, not just to political ads but any sort of controversial content that might catch fire. Stopping the spread of disinformation is a perpetual problem. Thankfully, we are now building intelligent tools that can help. Jae Lee is CEO and cofounder of TwelveLabs.

The Witcher 4 Wants To Be The GTA 6 Of The Witcher Franchise

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Gamespot)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there's been a massive gap between newly introduced entries in The Witcher series, and for The Witcher 4, developer CD Projekt Red aims to make it the GTA 6 of the series, with a noticeable leap in quality.
  • There's been a massive gap between upcoming entries in The Witcher series, and for The Witcher 4, developer CD Projekt Red aims to make it the GTA 6 of the series, with a noticeable leap in quality.
  • "First of all, obviously this is a call about us, not about Rockstar," CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski (via Eurogamer).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there's been a massive gap between newly introduced entries in The Witcher series, and for The Witcher 4, developer CD Projekt Red aims to make it the GTA 6 of the series, with a noticeable leap in quality. In its Q3 earnings call, the studio notes it has been inspired by the technological and gameplay advancements Rockstar Games has made with GTA 6--especially when compared to 2013's GTA 5--and hopes players will feel the same way when they jump into The Witcher 4. "First of all, obviously this is a call about us, not about Rockstar," CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski (via Eurogamer). "But I do understand the connection here. Having stated that, I'm not going to make a deep-dive and a full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6. But of course we did look at the game; we did see the differences. We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4--I think so, yes. It's been 11 years; we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4." https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4c1rokekgnY When The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt was first released in 2015, it was hailed for raising the bar for open-world adventure games. Its side-quests were singled out for being narratively dense, full of micro-consequences, and on par with the main campaign missions. In the years since, numerous open-world games have used The Witcher 3 as a blueprint, with notable examples being the Assassin's Creed trilogy of Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla alongside Sony's Horizon Zero Dawn and Ghost of Tsushima. Eleven years later, that bar has been raised again with GTA 6, which offers emergent, player-driven open-world chaos through multiple systems. The world of The Witcher is naturally very different from the consumerism-focused setting of GTA 6, but if The Witcher 4 builds on its predecessor's strengths and adds more nuance to those gameplay mechanics, we could be in for something special. CDPR also said it's trying to make The Witcher 4 more appealing to mainstream audiences, but it hasn't detailed exactly how it prepares to do that. "Our games are different, and they require a certain different approach--we just do things differently than they do. But in terms of the ultimate effect, in terms of breaking out to the mass market awareness: This is for sure something we consider pivotal to whatever we're going to do with our marketing campaigns in the future," Nowakowski said. At the moment, over 500 people are working on The Witcher 4, and CDPR has signed a marketing agreement with PlayStation for the game ahead of its targeted 2028 release. The studio is also chipping away at Cyberpunk 2, but after the launch of GTA 6, the game's creative director joked about canceling it, saying Rockstar's game set a high standard for open-world games.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a 2026 Gartner survey, 87% of customers said companies using generative AI for customer service must provide access to a human agent.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

Every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

In a recent development, so how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:.

Sources indicate that if a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

It has been revealed that running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

Industry observers note that in hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

Recent findings suggest that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”.

According to recent reports, her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

In a recent development, “I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”.

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that “Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”.

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test aims, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

Sources indicate that “While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” remarked Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”.

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

In a recent development, “Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks fresh avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” noted Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”.

In a recent development, the workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and revealed by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

Sources indicate that “The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” said Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”.

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

According to recent reports, “We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she mentioned. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”.

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

In a recent development, “Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she noted. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”.

#98. Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says

Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.
  • AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.
  • This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret. This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic. Researchers interviewed 66 executives, managers, and employees at 58 of Anthropic’s corporate customers and found that many workers are reluctant to share their best AI tricks, citing reasons ranging from job security to more leisure time. The practice has frustrated managers looking to exploit AI-driven efficiencies. The report quotes one exasperated executive saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.” AI hoarding is a new form of the age-old workplace phenomenon of knowledge hiding, in which employees deliberately withhold information from their coworkers to retain a competitive edge. Employees in the AI age have even more at stake: their jobs. If the trick they develop is powerful enough, they might render themselves redundant. And even for those whose jobs are secure, revealing a time-saving trick might just mean they are assigned more work. That raises a thorny question for business leaders: How do you incentivize employees to help automate their own jobs? Employers hoping to discourage AI hoarding may need to rethink how they measure and reward productivity. Otherwise, employees might realize that their most valuable professional asset is something they’re better off keeping secret.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PC modders are racing to get GTA 6 playable on PC after the leak of the game's complete Xbox build, but so far it doesn't look too promising. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games haven't been sitting idle either, as one of the leads behind the Project Leonida Discord group claimed in now-deleted social media posts that they were stepping away from the mammoth task of getting GTA 6 to run on PC. Project Leonida has also been taken down, but it's not the only group trying to get GTA 6 running outside of PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA None of these groups have succeeded yet, and as Twitter user Chasm detailed online, maybe relying heavily on AI tools isn't the way to go. Dev streams have been full of people leveraging generative AI tools to do something, with several prompts being absolute gems of wishful thinking. Here's a snippet of what people have been throwing at Google's Antigravity, while butchering the English language: Continue working and do apply ever part of the code make no mistakes You need todo one thing at a time not a little bit of everything we need all the game start like the rockstar launch so on that stuff, not in game stuff yet work faster there has to be a faster way to iterate than this Even with an army of enthusiasts throwing prompts and cash at generative AI, a copied version of GTA 6 still seems far out of reach. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick commented in March that the idea of using AI and simply pushing a button to make a hit game was "laughable," and he referenced the music industry, which is grappling with a flood of AI slop to top streaming platforms. "Right now [in music] there are programs that allow you to put out a prompt and get a professionally recorded song spit back out at you. It sounds like a song, but I defy you to listen to it more than once. It's great to send as a greeting card to your partner on their birthday, but that's about it," Zelnick said. Whatever progress is made in the GTA 6 PC port scene, don't expect it to last long before Take-Two's lawyers pounce. The publisher hasn't shied away from protecting its IP in the past, and takedown notices for any future GTA 6-related projects seem likely. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

“I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making significant decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”.

The actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative rolled out this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

Sources indicate that at the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A newly introduced docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

According to recent reports, and then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

The stakes are significant. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

An analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common challenges, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

It has been revealed that 1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching new customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

In a recent development, “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she stated. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

According to recent reports, 2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she remarked.

Recent findings suggest that 3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

Industry observers note that “Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she mentioned.

4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

“You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she stated. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

Industry observers note that to see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the big-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • In a recent development, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

In a recent development, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A latest investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Sources indicate that delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

In a recent development, many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

According to recent reports, before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants indicated some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can rapidly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

It has been revealed that NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

#88. Latest Update: Innovation doesn’t scale on its own

Latest Update: Innovation doesn’t scale on its own

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear.
  • I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear.
  • Industry observers note that anyone who has spent time around young children knows the noise—the laughter, the crying, the constant motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear. Anyone who has spent time around young children knows the noise—the laughter, the crying, the constant motion. When malnutrition has reached a crisis point, that noise is gone. Children sit still in ways they aren’t supposed to. That stillness is one of the first signals something is wrong. Intervening early is critical. Health workers can use the most basic tools to measure a child’s upper arm to quickly assess nutritional health. The intervention is surprisingly simple: providing a small packet filled with peanut paste, milk powder, and a precise blend of micronutrients. A six-week course of the packets follows and it can alter the entire trajectory of their life. Thirty years later, it remains one of the world’s most effective tools in global health. WHY PRODUCT INNOVATION ISN’T ENOUGH There’s a persistent bias toward the new in how innovation gets funded. Moonshots are celebrated and disruption gets rewarded. The assumption is that the most transformative solutions involve the most sophisticated technology. Breakthrough innovation is crucial, but collective expertise, commitment, and coordination are critical to scaling. Ready-to-use therapeutic food, known as RUTF, is one of these breakthrough innovations. Before it existed, treating severe acute malnutrition meant hospital stays and clinical formulas most families couldn’t access. RUTF changed the equation with a shelf-stable, portable product that didn’t require refrigeration. A caregiver could administer it at home. A health worker could distribute it in a village with no running water. Its success was never tied to a single organization. Over the past three decades, it has been adopted by governments, humanitarian organizations, and health systems around the world. For business leaders, the lesson is familiar. The challenge is rarely inventing the solution. It’s building the conditions that allow it to scale. THE OVERLOOKED NECESSITY We often think of innovation as a product challenge. Build the right solution and impact follows. But scale rarely works that way. What determines success is everything surrounding the innovation: distribution, financing, trust, incentives, and infrastructure. Getting RUTF to a child who needs it is more than a point A to point B challenge. It requires identifying malnutrition before it becomes irreversible, especially in the first 1,000 days of life. It necessitates a health worker who can make that call—and in many communities, that person isn’t a credentialed clinician. It is often a minimally compensated local community member. It requires supply chains that reach remote places where businesses don’t. It depends on coordination between governments, manufacturers, and health systems. If any one of those fails, a child goes untreated. RUTF endures because the ecosystem built around it proved strong enough to sustain it through political shifts, funding disruptions, and supply chain crises. That infrastructure is consistently underestimated and consistently underfunded. THE NEXT INNOVATION The next breakthrough for nutrition is a systems innovation—one that closes the gap between what works and what reaches people at scale. The UNICEF-led Child Nutrition Fund puts that idea into action. By bringing together government leadership, financing, and technical expertise, it helps accelerate the scale-up of proven nutrition interventions while strengthening the systems behind them. In doing so, it helps bridge critical gaps in nutrition services and supports country-led efforts to save lives, build resilience, and improve outcomes for women and children. That’s the innovation this moment requires—a smarter way to build and sustain the systems that deliver it. Don’t just back a product. Back the infrastructure that makes it possible. The right product can change a child’s life. The ecosystem is what gets it there, and scale is what reshapes the future. The leaders who understand this invest in the breakthroughs and the systems that make breakthroughs last. Michele Walsh is executive vice president and chief philanthropy officer of UNICEF USA.

Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet firm.
  • Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet firm. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the latest cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

According to recent reports, still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game strategy to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

In a recent development, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

Sources indicate that within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” consumers on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

Screen time got your brain fried? Try a ‘brain stack’

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every few months, like clockwork, a upcoming analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones.
  • Every few months, like clockwork, a latest analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones.
  • The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every few months, like clockwork, a upcoming analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones. . .and of course, document the process for social media. The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling. Online, thousands of people have proudly shared their “stacks”. One popular creator, Mandy Rulez, regularly shares timelapse videos of her brain stacks before work, starting her morning with nearby stacks of non-digital activities, like journaling, before moving on to a sudoku, a crossword, and finally a quick ten pages of reading. Other creators are also incorporating timers into the mix. For example, a 12-minute brain dump in a spiral notebook, followed by ten minutes of planning, 15 minutes of puzzles, 20 minutes of coloring. Total brain stack: one hour. Brain stacking is a continuation of the “analog bag” trend earlier this year (otherwise known as, well, simply “doing things.”) But we’re in an era when “brain rot” and “doomscrolling” have become part of our everyday lexicon, so it’s easy to see the appeal. Gen Z, after all, are the ones embracing dumb phones and buying up Bricks in an effort to reduce their screen time. The idea of “habit stacking” has existed in the world of self-help for years, and involves stacking new habits to existing ones. More recently, bedtime stacking, as well as peptide stacking, have emerged as online trends. Then there’s goal stacking and income stacking. Clearly, queuing up back-to-back activities (and, ideally, literally and physically stacking them in a pile to work through) resonates with people on social media. In a year where “maxxing” was crowned Dictionary.com’s word of the year, it’s unsurprising that a single activity alone is not enough—instead, we must stack them one on top of each other to reach our max potential. (There is also the visually pleasing element of the stack when it comes to posting online.)  That does not mean there’s anything inherently wrong with brain stacking. Having a range of activities close at hand means you are far more likely to be intentional with your spare time. And a 2024 study found just five minutes of fiction reading can reduce stress by up to 20%, as well as sharpening concentration and problem-solving skills. Reading is also associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease. But recent findings from a collaboration among researchers at Clemson University, the Medical University of South Carolina, and Penn State found that “brain-training” activities, such as crosswords, sudoku, memory games and adult coloring books, are not equally effective for everyone. College students, for example, often show only modest benefits from such brain-training activities compared with older adults who live relatively sedentary lifestyles. There’s also no specific research that supports the brain stacking method of working your way through a queue of a certain number of tasks, or spending a specific amount of time on each. If you find yourself absorbed in a book, or reach a flow state in your writing, don’t feel bound to 10-minute sprints and then moving onto the next brain-boosting activity. That mentioned? Any amount of time away from your screens is time well spent.

Industry observers note that operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

Recent findings suggest that three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

It has been revealed that the affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Recent findings suggest that each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation issue while the project remained closed.

It has been revealed that the cost revealed up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

Industry observers note that the extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

The billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing challenges that had nothing to do with the migration.

As the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

It has been revealed that this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

It has been revealed that those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Recent findings suggest that once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

Industry observers note that the sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The firm did three things:.

It has been revealed that those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

The acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

Industry observers note that for the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration problems before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

According to recent reports, billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the upcoming exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still demonstrated a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

Sources indicate that the company also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Industry observers note that support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

Sources indicate that the technical issue was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

According to recent reports, A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

Recent findings suggest that no one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

According to recent reports, that’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level. Some are saying it's too easy. Rockstar boss Rob Nelson has now entered the conversation, telling Destructoid that Rockstar's data showed that GTA 4 was "a little too punishing in places" and GTA 5 was "perhaps too easy." So with GTA 6, the team trying to "land somewhere in the middle." GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition. That said, players can adjust things like aiming controls, while players can unlock cheat codes to make the game easier or harder. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dJDf76QVv70 Design producer Scott Mitchell, meanwhile, said the fail states in GTA 6 were designed to feel "appropriate." “We wanted to keep things open and not limit the players’ use of mechanics, such as stealth, but we did also want to make sure we retained the cinematic, high production value, explosive sequences that we’re known for, and people expect. It feels like we’ve managed to strike a good balance," he explained. Also in the interview, Nelson said figuring out the difficulty level for GTA 6 is itself challenging because the designers themselves know enemy positions better than anyone after playing and testing the game so much. "There’s a real process in unpicking some of that to create an experience most players will be able to enjoy, rather than endure," Nelson said. "The game is so big, and has such a wide range of content that we can really lean into that, making certain open-world content--compounds and fronts for example---more difficult, to give players seeking a challenge something to sink their teeth into as well.” GTA 6 released on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

It has been revealed that the U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Latest Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Industry observers note that fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA unveiled its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

According to recent reports, “We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” stated Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”.

According to recent reports, under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

Recent findings suggest that “Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”.

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

It has been revealed that “GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”.

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

Following his recent resignation from the company and his return as CEO earlier this week, Jensen Huang has received a glowing statement of support from Denny's, the chain where he famously began his working life before founding Nvidia. The diner chain Denny's posted a 200-word statement to X in which it sought to maintain its links to the Nvidia founder, saying that there are "some things you just don’t take off the menu." Notably, the chain also noted that it has restored a plaque commemorating the occasion to "where it belongs," days after it was removed amid growing controversy over Huang and his affair with former Megaspeed employee Alice Huang. Megaspeed is now under criminal investigation over its involvement in bypassing U.S. export controls relating to Nvidia's advanced AI chips. It's also believed that Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, may also be a spy with connections to China's Ministry of State Security.

Despite all of that, Denny's has very much hitched its trailer to Huang and his reputation, for better or worse. The diner's statement ends by reminding him that his booth "is always waiting and the coffee's on," although it's unclear whether he'll be able to make time for a visit between his upcoming visit to Congress to discuss the last few weeks' goings-on and joining board meetings with U.S. President Donald Trump. There is good news for Huang, though, even if he's found to have broken the law during his trysts with the suspected spy. Trump says that a pardon is "always an option," meaning Huang could be free to visit all the Denny's diners he wants to in the future.

It has been revealed that as for Nvidia, its share price has suffered the same fate as other tech stocks in recent weeks. It rallied after initially nosediving around the time of Huang's resignation, but has since continued its downward trajectory, having fallen almost 2.4 percentage points in the last five days and over 30 points in the last month.

#68. Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1187 w)

Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Fastcompany)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that fresh workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.
  • Upcoming workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.
  • As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fresh workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work. That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations. When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t. A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) remarked they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption. Only 39% of people have built AI into a standardized way of working, according to the LSE Inclusion Initiative and Protiviti report. Those who have reported saving 27% of time in their work week with AI, compared with 14% for those who haven’t. Gen Z is far more likely to have been AI-trained in the past year compared with their baby boomer colleagues. AI-trained employees report saving 22% of their working hours, compared with 13% for those left to figure it out alone. And what exactly happens to all that extra time saved by AI? More time for more work, of course. And it’s causing what researchers are calling “workload creep”. “AI is creating meaningful productivity gains, but the bigger opportunity is how organizations use the capacity it creates,” said Matt Duncan, managing director at Protiviti, in the press release. “Simply absorbing those gains into existing workloads leaves much of AI’s potential untapped.” Researchers at Boston Consulting Group found that 14% of people who use AI workflows requiring a high degree of oversight experience “AI brain fry.” This mental fog and inability to focus can result in more mistakes at work, and even employees considering quitting altogether. AI or not, job performance is still dependent on people, at least for now. And the LSE and Protiviti report found no consistent association between an employee’s perceived performance and their AI adoption, access, training or workflow integration. Instead, performance stayed tied to confidence in solving problems, conscientiousness, resilience and willingness to learn. As AI continues to become embedded in everyday work, organizations need to focus on whether it is actually helping employees be more efficient at work, or simply creating time to pile more work on their plates. “Leaders should think deliberately about where that capacity can create the most value, whether that means tackling higher-value work, improving quality or giving employees greater space to solve problems and innovate,” said Duncan. “The goal shouldn’t just be doing more work faster, but using AI to change what people are able to accomplish.”.
